landmarks.name: Okavango Delta
landmarks.writeup: A vast inland delta known for its rich biodiversity and unique ecosystem, attracting numerous wildlife and bird species.

wiki.extract: The Okavango Delta or Okavango Grassland is a vast inland delta in Botswana formed where the Okavango River reaches a tectonic trough at an elevation of 930–1,000 m (3,050–3,280 ft) in the central part of the endorheic basin of the Kalahari Desert.

landmarks.name: Chobe National Park
landmarks.writeup: Famous for its large elephant population and diverse wildlife, it is one of Africa's premier game-viewing destinations.

wiki.extract: Chobe National Park is Botswana's first national park, and also its most biologically diverse. The park contains the wetlands of the Chobe River, which flows into Victoria Falls and the Zambezi to the East. Located in the north of the country, the park is part of the Kavango–Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area, and partially borders Namibia's Caprivi Strip. It is Botswana's third largest park.

landmarks.name: Tsodilo Hills
landmarks.writeup: A UNESCO World Heritage site featuring ancient rock art and spiritual significance to local communities.

wiki.extract: The Tsodilo Hills are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (WHS), consisting of rock art, rock shelters, depressions, and caves in Botswana, Southern Africa.

cultural_events.name: Dithubaruba Cultural Festival
cultural_events.writeup: An annual event celebrating Tswana culture through traditional music, dance, and storytelling.

wiki.extract: The Dithubaruba Cultural Festival is one of the national events celebrated in Botswana and is also marked in the Botswana Calendar of Events. It aims to promote Kweneng cultural heritage and create leisure time for the community.

food_writeup: Botswana's cuisine features staple foods like sorghum and maize, with traditional dishes such as seswaa (slow-cooked shredded beef) and bogobe (millet porridge).
brief_history: Botswana gained independence from Britain in 1966. It has since maintained a stable democracy and experienced steady economic growth, largely due to diamond mining.

commentary.inflation_management: The Bank of Botswana has one of Africa's better inflation records, operating a crawling peg of the pula against a rand-and-SDR basket with a 3-6% objective range. Inflation spiked to 12.6% in 2008 on the global commodity boom and 11.6% in 2006, but the bank brought it down steadily to 1.9% in 2020, the series low. The 2022 shock pushed it back to 12.2%, and policy tightened in response; inflation fell to 5.1% in 2023 and 2.8% in both 2024 and 2025. The framework is credible and expectations are anchored, but with diamonds driving the economy, the real monetary risk is a terms-of-trade shock the exchange rate band cannot absorb.
commentary.debt_management: Botswana was long the textbook case of diamond-financed prudence: debt bottomed at 5.9% of GDP in 2007 and stayed near 20-25% through the 2010s, with large reserves in the Pula Fund. That era is ending. COVID pushed debt to 24.3% in 2020, and the 2024-25 diamond slump, as lab-grown stones and weak demand crushed De Beers sales, forced heavy borrowing: debt jumped to 32.8% in 2024 and a projected 38.6% in 2025, the series high. The government has drawn on reserves and issued domestic debt. Sustainability is not yet threatened, but the speed of the deterioration shows how a single-commodity fiscal model can unwind.

key_events.event: Global financial crisis crushed diamond demand; debt jumped from 7.8% to 21.8% of GDP as the government spent to cushion the economy.
COVID-19: diamond sales collapsed; GDP in USD terms fell to $15.6bn.
Post-COVID diamond rebound took GDP to a series high of $20.3bn; inflation spiked to 12.2%.
October 30 election: Duma Boko's UDC coalition ended 58 years of BDP rule amid anger over unemployment and the diamond downturn; diamond revenues slumped, forcing a wider deficit.
Prolonged diamond market weakness pushed public debt to a projected 38.6% of GDP, a record, as the new government faced depleted buffers.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: The base case is a slow, painful adjustment: diamond revenues are unlikely to return to 2022 levels, forcing either spending cuts, new revenue sources, or a permanently higher debt path. Upside depends on diversification (tourism, financial services) and a diamond market recovery; downside is a fiscal crisis if borrowing continues while reserves erode. Uncertainty is moderate-to-high: the 2024 political turnover was peaceful, but the new government's economic program is untested.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
